# Getting Started with ContextNet

**ContextNet** adapts [NicheNet](https://github.com/saeyslab/nichenetr)-style ligand-target prediction by using a **context-specific gene regulatory network (GRN)** inferred from sc-multiomic data or another regulatory-inference workflow. In practice, ContextNet asks whether a sender-cell ligand can explain a receiver-cell gene program through regulatory edges that are active in that context.

## Goal of Tutorial 01

This tutorial is a smoke test and object-model walkthrough. It uses a small synthetic example dataset included with the package. The expected result is simple by design: ligand `TGFB1` should rank above `FGF2` because the toy gene regulatory network connects `TGFB1` more strongly to the receiver target program.

The synthetic result should not be interpreted biologically. Its purpose is to show what files ContextNet expects, what objects it creates, what the printed output should look like, and how tables can be extracted for downstream analysis.

## What Is a Context-Specific Gene Regulatory Network (GRN)?

A **gene regulatory network (GRN)** describes which transcription factors regulate which target genes and how strongly those regulatory edges are supported. NicheNet uses a generic regulatory prior compiled from public knowledge. ContextNet replaces the regulatory-network component of that prior with a context-specific GRN inferred from matched single-cell RNA-seq and single-cell ATAC-seq or another upstream regulatory-inference workflow.

This matters because ligand-target prediction depends on the regulatory layer. If the GRN is generic, a ligand can be prioritized through regulatory edges that may not be active in the tissue, disease state, or cell population being studied. If the GRN is context-specific, the ligand-target matrix is constrained by the regulatory relationships observed in the profiled system.

ContextNet expects one of these GRN inputs:

| Input type | What it means | Typical source |
|------------|---------------|----------------|
| target-gene x transcription-factor matrix | Rows are target genes, columns are transcription factors, values are regulatory weights | context-specific GRN inference pipeline |
| edge table | One row per transcription-factor to target-gene edge | SCENIC+, Pando, custom models |
| package-specific object | Regulatory output already produced by another tool | SCENIC+, Pando |

The package importer normalizes those inputs into a `ContextGRN` object. The upstream context-specific GRN inference pipeline is documented at [settylab/context_specific_grn](https://github.com/settylab/context_specific_grn). ContextNet can also use a compatible matrix or edge table from another regulatory-inference workflow.

## Environment and Data Setup

Install ContextNet before starting this tutorial using the repository [installation instructions](../README.md#installation). The cells below only load packages, locate the included example dataset, and print the expected input files.

The notebook can be run from the repository root or from the `notebooks/` directory. The setup cell normalizes the working directory to the repository root so the same source works in Jupyter, JupyterLab, `nbconvert`, and RStudio.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_03, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(ContextNet)
    library(Seurat)
    library(nichenetr)
    library(ggplot2)
})

# ccflowR is optional. ContextNet should still run when only the river plot
# dependency is absent.
HAS_CCFLOWR <- requireNamespace("ccflowR", quietly = TRUE)
if (HAS_CCFLOWR) {
    suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ccflowR))
} else {
    message("ccflowR is not installed; the Sankey visualization cell will be skipped.")
}

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_family = "sans"))
```

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_04, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
check_ecosystem(verbose = TRUE)
```

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_05, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
PROJECT_DIR <- normalizePath(getwd(), mustWork = TRUE)
if (basename(PROJECT_DIR) == "notebooks" &&
    file.exists(file.path(PROJECT_DIR, "..", "DESCRIPTION"))) {
    PROJECT_DIR <- normalizePath(file.path(PROJECT_DIR, ".."), mustWork = TRUE)
}
if (!file.exists(file.path(PROJECT_DIR, "DESCRIPTION"))) {
    stop("Run this notebook from the ContextNet repository root or from the notebooks/ directory.")
}
setwd(PROJECT_DIR)

# Print project-relative paths so public tutorial output does not expose
# machine-specific directories.
display_path <- function(path) {
    normalized <- normalizePath(path, mustWork = FALSE)
    root <- normalizePath(PROJECT_DIR, mustWork = TRUE)
    if (startsWith(normalized, root)) {
        return(sub("^/", "", substring(normalized, nchar(root) + 1)))
    }
    paste0("<external>/", basename(normalized))
}

cat("Using project root:", basename(getwd()), "\n")

CACHE_DIR <- file.path(PROJECT_DIR, "data", "cache", "tutorial-01-outputs")
if (!dir.exists(CACHE_DIR)) dir.create(CACHE_DIR, recursive = TRUE)


SMOKE_DIR <- Sys.getenv(
    "CONTEXTNET_SMOKE_DIR",
    unset = file.path(PROJECT_DIR, "inst", "extdata", "contextnet_smoke")
)
GRN_FILE <- file.path(SMOKE_DIR, "gene_x_tf.csv")
SEURAT_FILE <- file.path(SMOKE_DIR, "seurat_obj.rds")
NICHENET_DB <- SMOKE_DIR

# The toy receiver program is hard-coded so the smoke-test result is
# deterministic across installations.
SENDER <- c("sender_a", "sender_b")
RECEIVER <- "receiver"
GENESET_OI <- c("SERPINE1", "CDKN1A")
GROUP_COL <- "cell_type"

stopifnot(file.exists(GRN_FILE), file.exists(SEURAT_FILE), dir.exists(NICHENET_DB))
cat("Example data directory:", display_path(SMOKE_DIR), "\n")
cat("GRN file:", display_path(GRN_FILE), "\n")
cat("Seurat file:", display_path(SEURAT_FILE), "\n")
cat("Toy NicheNet database:", display_path(NICHENET_DB), "\n")
cat("ccflowR available:", HAS_CCFLOWR, "\n")
```

## Step 1: Inspect the Smoke-Test Inputs

The included example dataset contains all inputs needed for a minimal ContextNet run:

- `gene_x_tf.csv`: a toy context-specific gene regulatory network (GRN).
- `seurat_obj.rds`: a tiny Seurat object with two sender populations, one receiver population, and one reference population.
- `lr_network_human_21122021.rds` and `weighted_networks_nsga2r_final.rds`: tiny NicheNet-compatible prior files.

The example dataset is synthetic. It is useful for installation testing because it is small, deterministic, and fully shareable.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_07, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
seurat_obj <- readRDS(SEURAT_FILE)

cat("Seurat object:", nrow(seurat_obj), "genes x", ncol(seurat_obj), "cells\n")
cat("Metadata columns:", paste(colnames(seurat_obj@meta.data), collapse = ", "), "\n")
print(table(seurat_obj[[GROUP_COL]][, 1]))

head(seurat_obj@meta.data)
```

The printed table confirms that the toy object has four cell populations. `sender_a` and `sender_b` express ligands, `receiver` expresses the target program, and `reference` gives a comparison population. In a full analysis, these metadata columns should encode biologically meaningful cell types, conditions, samples, and receiver populations.

## Step 2: Import the Context-Specific Gene Regulatory Network (GRN)

`import_grn()` reads the target-gene x transcription-factor matrix and returns a `ContextGRN`. This object stores the regulatory evidence before any NicheNet propagation has happened. At this point, the edges are transcription-factor to target-gene relationships, not ligand-target predictions.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_10, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
grn <- import_grn(GRN_FILE, verbose = FALSE)

cat("Object class:", class(grn), "\n")
cat("Transcription factors:", length(tfs(grn)), "\n")
cat("Target genes:", length(targets(grn)), "\n")
cat("Regulatory edges:", length(grn), "\n")

head(edges(grn))
```

Interpret this output before continuing. A useful `ContextGRN` should have non-zero edges, recognizable transcription-factor symbols, target genes that overlap the expression object, and enough density to propagate signal. In the smoke fixture, the expected edges are `SMAD3 -> SERPINE1/CDKN1A` and `FOS -> MMP1/JUNB`.

## Step 3: Integrate the GRN with NicheNet Priors

`integrate_networks()` combines three layers:

1. ligand-receptor prior edges,
2. intracellular signaling prior edges,
3. the context-specific transcription-factor to target-gene GRN.

The result is a `ContextNetwork`. Its central data structure is a ligand-target matrix: rows are target genes, columns are ligands, and values are propagated regulatory-potential scores. This object is reusable across many sender/receiver analyses from the same biological context.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_13, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
network <- integrate_networks(
    grn,
    nichenet_database = NICHENET_DB,
    mode = "replace",      # use the context-specific GRN as the regulatory layer
    damping_factor = 0.5,    # propagation damping used by personalized PageRank
    ltf_cutoff = 0,          # keep all toy ligand-TF paths for the deterministic check
    verbose = FALSE
)

ltm <- ligand_target_matrix(network)
cat("Object class:", class(network), "\n")
cat("Ligand-target matrix:", nrow(ltm), "targets x", ncol(ltm), "ligands\n")
round(ltm[c("SERPINE1", "CDKN1A", "MMP1", "JUNB"), , drop = FALSE], 3)
```

The matrix should show stronger `TGFB1` weights for `SERPINE1` and `CDKN1A`, and stronger `FGF2` weights for `MMP1` and `JUNB`. That is the built-in positive control for this smoke test. In a real dataset, the same matrix is the ContextNet-specific replacement for NicheNet's default ligand-target matrix.

## Step 4: Predict Ligand Activity for One Receiver Program

For the smoke test, the receiver target genes are provided directly with `geneset_oi = c("SERPINE1", "CDKN1A")`. This avoids running differential expression on a toy object and makes the expected output deterministic. In a full analysis, ContextNet can use either a curated receiver gene set or differentially expressed genes from a cell-type or condition comparison.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_16, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
result <- predict_ligand_activity_nichenet(
    object = seurat_obj,
    network = network,
    sender = SENDER,              # sender populations that express candidate ligands
    receiver = RECEIVER,          # receiver population carrying the target program
    geneset_oi = GENESET_OI,      # deterministic toy receiver program
    group_col = GROUP_COL,        # metadata column containing cell-population labels
    top_n_ligands = 2,       # retain both toy ligands so the ranking is visible
    top_n_targets = 4,       # retain all toy targets so target support is visible
    nichenet_database = NICHENET_DB,
    verbose = TRUE
)

cat("Object class:", class(result), "\n")
cat("Top ligands:", paste(top_ligands(result), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Top targets:", paste(top_targets(result), collapse = ", "), "\n")

ligand_activities(result)
```

The expected top ligand is `TGFB1`. The most important columns are:

- `test_ligand`: the candidate upstream ligand being scored.
- `aupr`: area under the precision-recall curve for recovering the receiver gene set. Higher values mean the ligand's predicted targets better recover the target program.
- `aupr_corrected`: AUPR after correcting for the baseline positive rate.
- `pearson`: correlation between predicted ligand-target regulatory potential and the receiver gene-set label.

For this fixture, `TGFB1` is intentionally connected to `SERPINE1` and `CDKN1A`, so it should rank above `FGF2`.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_18, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
ligand_target_links(result)
```

The ligand-target link table explains why the ligand ranked highly. In the example dataset, `TGFB1 -> SERPINE1` and `TGFB1 -> CDKN1A` have higher regulatory-potential weights than the corresponding `FGF2` links. In a real analysis, inspect this table before making biological claims from a ranked ligand list.

## Step 5: Visualize the Main Outputs

The bar plot summarizes ligand activity. The heatmap-like tile plot shows which ligand-target links support the ranking. These plots are intentionally simple so the smoke-test output is easy to compare across installations.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_21, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
activities <- ligand_activities(result)
activities$test_ligand <- factor(
    activities$test_ligand,
    levels = rev(activities$test_ligand[order(activities$aupr)])
)

ggplot(activities, aes(x = aupr, y = test_ligand)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#3B6FB6") +
    labs(
        x = "Ligand activity (AUPR)",
        y = "Ligand",
        title = "Smoke test ligand ranking"
    )
```

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_22, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
links <- ligand_target_links(result)

ggplot(links, aes(x = ligand, y = target, fill = weight)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white") +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F2F2F2", high = "orange") +
    labs(
        x = "Ligand",
        y = "Receiver target gene",
        fill = "Regulatory potential",
        title = "Ligand-target support for the smoke-test program"
    )
```

## Optional Path-Level Visualization with ccflowR

`ccflowR` is an optional visualization package for Sankey or river plots of cell-cell communication. It helps when a table of ligand activities is no longer enough: for example, when the goal is to see which sender cell types, ligands, receptors, and receiver cells form the highest-priority paths.

ContextNet prepares the path table with `prepare_for_ccflowr()` and `combine_sankey_data()`. If `ccflowR` is not installed, the core ContextNet analysis still works; only this visualization is skipped.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_24, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
# prepare_for_ccflowr() expands the ContextResult into sender-ligand-receptor-
# receiver paths. The toy dataset is tiny, so min_cells is intentionally low.
sankey_raw <- prepare_for_ccflowr(
    result,
    expression_data = seurat_obj,
    network = network,
    top_n_ligands = 2,       # retain both toy ligands in the Sankey input
    group_col = GROUP_COL,
    min_cells = 5
)

# threshold_quantile = 0 keeps every toy path so the printed table is stable.
sankey_data <- combine_sankey_data(sankey_raw, threshold_quantile = 0)

cat("ccflowR input rows:", nrow(sankey_data), "\n")
head(sankey_data)
```

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_25, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
if (HAS_CCFLOWR) {
    cell_colors <- c(
        sender_a = "#3B6FB6", sender_b = "#8B5A2B",
        receiver = "#2F8F5B", reference = "#999999"
    )

    sankey_plot <- suppressMessages(
        ccflowR::sankey_plot(sankey_data, colors = cell_colors) +
            ccflowR::sankey_colors(by = "receiver") +
            ccflowR::sankey_alpha(0.65) +
            ccflowR::sankey_title("ContextNet smoke-test paths") +
            ccflowR::sankey_font(family = "Arial", size = 12) +
            ccflowR::sankey_layout(width = 760, height = 520)
    )
    print(sankey_plot)
} else {
    message("Skipping Sankey plot because ccflowR is not installed.")
}
```

Read the Sankey plot as a prioritized path-level hypothesis, not as proof of physical communication. A real path needs additional support from ligand expression, receptor expression, spatial proximity, perturbation, or orthogonal validation.

## Object Model Summary

ContextNet uses three main S4 objects. The important point is that each object answers a different question.

| Object | Created by | Question it answers | What to inspect |
|--------|------------|--------------------|-----------------|
| `ContextGRN` | `import_grn()` | What regulatory edges are active in this context? | `edges()`, `tfs()`, `targets()`, `regulons()` |
| `ContextNetwork` | `integrate_networks()` | How do ligands propagate to target genes through this context-specific network? | `ligand_target_matrix()`, `ligands()`, `integration_params()` |
| `ContextResult` | `predict_ligand_activity_nichenet()` | Which ligands explain this receiver gene program? | `ligand_activities()`, `top_ligands()`, `ligand_target_links()`, `parameters()` |

The code below prints compact summaries of those objects so local output can be compared with the expected shape.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_28, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
object_summary <- list(
    ContextGRN = list(
        class = class(grn),
        n_edges = length(grn),
        n_tfs = length(tfs(grn)),
        n_targets = length(targets(grn))
    ),
    ContextNetwork = list(
        class = class(network),
        ltm_dim = paste(dim(ligand_target_matrix(network)), collapse = " x "),
        ligands = paste(ligands(network), collapse = ", "),
        mode = integration_params(network)$mode
    ),
    ContextResult = list(
        class = class(result),
        top_ligands = paste(top_ligands(result), collapse = ", "),
        n_ligand_activity_rows = nrow(ligand_activities(result)),
        n_ligand_target_links = nrow(ligand_target_links(result))
    )
)

object_summary
```

## Troubleshooting the Smoke Test

| Symptom | Likely cause | What to check |
|---------|--------------|---------------|
| `library(ContextNet)` fails | The notebook kernel is not using the installed ContextNet environment | Re-register and select the `ContextNet R` kernel, then rerun `check_ecosystem(verbose = TRUE)`. |
| The example files are missing | The notebook is not running from the ContextNet repository or the package was installed without `inst/extdata` | Run from the repository root or check `system.file("extdata", "contextnet_smoke", package = "ContextNet")`. |
| The ligand-target matrix has zero rows or columns | The GRN, ligand-receptor prior, or weighted prior files do not overlap | Confirm that `gene_x_tf.csv`, `lr_network_human_21122021.rds`, and `weighted_networks_nsga2r_final.rds` come from the same example directory. |
| `TGFB1` is not the top ligand | The toy GRN or toy NicheNet prior was changed | Recreate the example data with `inst/scripts/create_smoke_data.R` or reinstall the package. |
| The Sankey cell is skipped | `ccflowR` is not installed | Install [ccflowR](https://github.com/settylab/ccflowR), then rerun only the optional Sankey cells. Core ContextNet output should already be available. |

## What to Do Next

If this notebook runs successfully, the installation is functional for the core ContextNet workflow. Next steps depend on the available data:

- Use Tutorial 02 for a real Seurat object and a context-specific GRN in a single-tissue epithelial-subtype analysis.
- Use Tutorial 03 for differential cell-cell communication analysis across conditions.
- Replace the smoke-test `gene_x_tf.csv` with a study-specific gene regulatory network (GRN), and replace the smoke-test Seurat object with the expression object for the study.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_30, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
session_pkgs <- c("ContextNet", "Seurat", "nichenetr", "multinichenetr", "ggplot2", "ccflowR")
cat("R version:", R.version.string, "\n")
for (pkg in session_pkgs) {
    if (requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
        cat(pkg, "version:", as.character(utils::packageVersion(pkg)), "\n")
    } else {
        cat(pkg, "version: not installed\n")
    }
}
```
